title: A day accounted for
hookLine: Seneca gives his day: a cold plunge, a short run, dry bread, a nap (Letters 83)

lines: WHAT DO YOU DO ALL DAY?
A DAY IN AN OLD PHILOSOPHER'S LIFE.
cards: What do you actually do all day? What time do you get up? What do you eat?
It's what people ask anyone whose life they're curious about, and it's what Lucilius has asked Seneca.

In the eighty-third letter, Seneca answers, hour by hour, with surprising honesty and quite a lot of humor at his own expense. What comes back is a day in the life of an aging Roman philosopher, and it's very ordinary.

teach.h: LIVE AS IF IN PLAIN SIGHT.
teach.b: We should live, Seneca says, as if in plain sight, as if God could look into our hearts at any time. So he'll watch himself and review his day, which he calls a most useful practice.
Today, he says, is whole: nobody stole any of it.
He's taken up a little running, with a young slave named Pharius as his partner. They're at the same turning point, he jokes, since both are losing teeth, and soon he won't be able to keep up.
Seneca was once a great cold-water bather. He used to greet the first of January with a plunge into the canal. Then he moved to the Tiber.
Then to a tub. And now, he confesses, it's a tub the sun has warmed, on his bravest days.

teach.h: DRY BREAD AND A SHORT NAP.
teach.b: Lunch is dry bread, no table needed, so simple there's no washing of hands afterward. Then a very short nap. Nothing heroic.
He doesn't polish the day. He shows the decline, the jokes, the plain bread. Accounting for a day like that isn't about judging it.
It's about seeing where it actually went.

how: Some Stoic practitioners write a plain account of their day in the evening, noting where the hours went without praising or scolding themselves.

o: a day spent in hard training for a race
a holiday when Romans plunged into cold water
a whole day, with none of it stolen

s: Seneca still takes an ice-cold plunge every day in old age
he confesses he went from canal to river to tub to warm water.
Seneca says nobody stole any part of this day
Seneca's lunch was a grand dinner party
dry bread, no table, no need to wash hands.

games.q: Lucilius asks what you do all day. you're an aging philosopher who's slowed down a lot. what do you write?
o: a heroic schedule to inspire him.
the honest timetable, including the warm bath and the nap.
games.why: Seneca reports it all, with jokes about his teeth and his softening plunge: an honest account, not a polished one.

practice: Walk back through today so far, hour by hour, the way Seneca does: when you woke, what came first, what you ate, where the middle of the day went. Don't polish it and don't scold it.
Notice one hour that was wholly yours, and one that got stolen.

wordCard.voice: Dies solidus. Latin for an unbroken day: Seneca reports his own, hour by hour, a run, a plunge, dry bread, a nap, to see where it went. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: an unbroken day. Seneca says in Letters 83.3 that today is unbroken, with nothing stolen from it.

carryVoice: Your line: my day, honestly. Even the bread and the nap count. That's today, accounted for.
